sections.title: 4 An independent finite proof in Lean

html:
Full-cycle commutators in the Rubik’s Cube group

Ruimin Yan
(November 26, 2026)

Abstract

Every even position of the fixed-centre Rubik’s Cube is a single commutator, by a theorem of Timothy Sun. We show that both factors can be required to induce an eight-cycle on the corners and a twelve-cycle on the edges. Each factor then has exact order 24. We give two proofs. The first deduces the factorization from a long-cycle theorem of Bader, Böhmler and Wegener by lifting permutations through the corner and edge orientation modules. For a fixed pair of edge cycles, the only obstruction to lifting all orientations is that the cycles induce the same alternating bipartition. The second proof, formalized in Lean 4, verifies finite certificates for the position cycle types and treats pure edge flips separately.

1 The restricted commutator map

Let G be the group of the ordinary 3×3×3 Rubik’s Cube, with the six centres fixed and unmarked. Write G+ for the subgroup of positions inducing even permutations on both the corner slots and the edge slots. We compose actions from right to left and put [A,B]=A⁢B⁢A−1⁢B−1. The sign of the corner permutation is a homomorphism on G, so every commutator lies in G+. Sun proved the converse: every element of G+ is a single commutator [2, Theorem 18]. We ask how far one may restrict the two factors while retaining this image.

Let ℱ⊆G consist of the positions whose corner permutation is an 8-cycle and whose edge permutation is a 12-cycle. An element of ℱ moves every corner and every edge. The orientation increments of its pieces are subject to the usual legality conditions.

Theorem 1.1.

The map

ℱ×ℱ⟶G+,(A,B)⟼[A,B],

is surjective. Every member of ℱ has order 24.

For example, a position which flips just two edges and leaves every other piece fixed admits such a factorization. All position changes cancel in the commutator, even though both factors move every piece.

Prescribing the cycle types of commutator factors is a classical question for symmetric groups; see Vavpetič [3]. Bader, Böhmler and Wegener [1, Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 3.4] give the permutation input used in our first proof. Their signed-cycle theorem prescribes negative sign product on each factor. A legal edge action on the cube has positive sign product, since it flips an even number of edges. We use their positional construction and their bipartition argument on the even orientation space; the corner lift takes place in characteristic three. Section 4 describes a second proof of the same cube-group statement using explicit witnesses in dimensions eight and twelve. The two proofs have different dependencies.

2 Lifting a positional commutator

For m∈{2,3}, let In={0,…,n−1} and set

Vn,m={v∈𝔽mIn:∑i∈Invi=0}.

The pair (p,v), with p∈Sn and v∈Vn,m, sends an oriented piece (i,z) to (p⁢(i),z+vi). Thus the increment is indexed by the source slot. Write Hn,m for the group of these actions. The standard cubie-coordinate theorem identifies G with

{((p,v),(q,w))∈H8,3×H12,2:sgn⁡(p)=sgn⁡(q)}. (1)

Here v records corner twists and w records edge flips. The two zero-sum conditions and the equality of signs are also sufficient for face-turn reachability [2, §3].

For c∈Sn put (Δc⁢x)i=xc⁢(i)−xi. This map preserves Vn,m. Fix a target T=(t,u) and write A=(a,x), B=(b,y). The equality [A,B]=T is equivalent to A⁢B=T⁢B⁢A. Applying both sides to (i,0) gives the two conditions

a⁢b =t⁢b⁢a, (2)
Δb⁢x−Δa⁢y =u∘b⁢a. (3)

For example, the two increments before subtraction are yi+xb⁢(i) and xi+ya⁢(i)+ub⁢(a⁢(i)). This also proves sufficiency, since both actions add the initial orientation z. Once a,b have been chosen, the possible right-hand sides in (3) form the sum of the images of the two difference maps restricted to Vn,m.

Lemma 2.1.

If c is an n-cycle and m∤n, then Δc:Vn,m⟶Vn,m is an isomorphism.

Proof.

A vector fixed by an n-cycle is constant. A constant vector with value k has coordinate sum n⁢k, which vanishes only for k=0. The claim follows by equality of dimensions. ∎

For even n, let 𝒫⁢(c)={Rc,Bc} be the two orbits of c2 for an n-cycle c. The two classes alternate around the cycle. The following description of the binary difference map is the balanced-bipartition lemma of [1, Lemmas 5.4 and 5.6]; we give the argument in source-slot coordinates.

Lemma 2.2.

For even n≥4, in V=Vn,2 one has

im⁡(Δc|V)=Uc,Uc={w∈V:∑i∈Rcwi=0}.

This is a hyperplane of V. For n-cycles a,b, Ua+Ub=V if and only if 𝒫⁢(a)≠𝒫⁢(b).

Proof.

Summing Δc⁢x over Rc gives the sum of x over all slots in characteristic two. Thus the image is contained in Uc. A vector with ones at one red and one blue slot shows that Uc is a proper hyperplane. The kernel on V is the one-dimensional space of constant vectors, so the image and Uc both have dimension n−2. If two unordered bipartitions differ, two slots in the same class of one lie in different classes of the other. Their two-point indicator distinguishes the hyperplanes. Two distinct hyperplanes span V; identical bipartitions give the same proper hyperplane. ∎

3 Proof of the factorization

We use the following consequence of [1, Theorem 3.1 and Proposition 3.4]. For n≥6, each t∈An has a representation t=[a,b] with a,b both n-cycles. If n is even and t≠id, one can moreover arrange 𝒫⁢(a)≠𝒫⁢(b). For clarity, Proposition 3.4 there gives a representative of each nonidentity even cycle type using the standard cycle and a normalized parity-unstable cycle. A parity defect in the latter places a label in the opposite alternating class, so the two bipartitions differ. Their convention for the commutator is a−1⁢b−1⁢a⁢b; replacing both cycles by their inverses converts it to ours and preserves both bipartitions. Simultaneous conjugation then gives the prescribed t.

Proposition 3.1.

For (n,m)=(8,3) or (12,2), every (t,u)∈Hn,m with t∈An is a commutator of two elements whose position permutations are n-cycles.

Proof.

For the corners, choose 8-cycles a,b with t=[a,b]. Since 3∤8, Lemma 2.1 solves Δb⁢x=u∘b⁢a in V8,3; take y=0. This includes t=id, for which one can take a=b.

For the edges with t≠id, choose 12-cycles a,b with distinct alternating bipartitions as above. Lemma 2.2 shows that every balanced u∘b⁢a belongs to Ub+Ua. Consequently (3) has a solution with x,y∈V12,2.

It remains to produce a pure flip (id,u). Pair the ones of u among themselves, and the zeros among themselves. Both multiplicities are even, so this gives six disjoint pairs, including when u=0 or u is all ones. Let R be the union of any three pairs. It has six slots and ∑i∈Rui=0. Choose a cycle c alternating between R and its complement, and take a=b=c. Its square preserves R, hence u∘c2∈Uc. Lemma 2.2 now supplies x∈V12,2 with Δc⁢x=u∘c2; take y=0. This is the twelve-slot case of the support selection in [1, Lemma 6.6]. In all three cases (2) and (3) give the asserted commutator. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Apply Proposition 3.1 to the corner and edge components of g∈G+. Write these components as [Ac,Bc] and [Ae,Be]. The 8-cycle in Ac and the 12-cycle in Ae both have negative sign. Their offsets are balanced, so A=(Ac,Ae) belongs to G by (1). The same holds for B=(Bc,Be). Commutators are taken componentwise in the product, which gives [A,B]=g.

If (c,x)∈Hn,m has an n-cycle as its permutation, its n-th power fixes each slot and adds ∑ixi=0 at each slot. Every power acting trivially on positions has exponent divisible by n. Thus the corner and edge actions of any member of ℱ have exact orders 8 and 12, respectively. The order in their direct product is lcm⁡(8,12)=24. ∎

Corollary 3.2 (Sun’s single-commutator theorem).

G+ is the derived subgroup of G, and each of its elements is a single commutator in G.

Proof.

The corner sign kills every commutator, hence its kernel contains the derived subgroup. Theorem 1.1 puts every element of that kernel in the image of the commutator map. ∎

Example 3.3 (The superflip).

Number the corner and edge slots cyclically, starting at zero, and let cn⁢(i)=i+1modn. Give A and B the same two position cycles c8,c12. Give both zero corner offsets; on edges take x=0 for A and yi=imod2 for B. Exactly six entries of y are nonzero. The left side of (3) is the all-ones edge vector, and the position commutator is trivial. Thus [A,B] flips every edge in place and fixes the corners. This pair is explicit in the accompanying formalization.

4 An independent finite proof in Lean

The ancillary development proves Theorem 1.1 in the group (1). It replaces the cited long-cycle construction by finite witnesses and checks the orientation lifts directly. Its declaration CubeComm.every_even_cube asserts membership of the two witnesses in the legal group, their full cycles, their exact orders and their commutator equation. The identification of (1) with the face-turn group uses the classical reachability theorem.

For each position cycle type, choose a representative t. A row specifies full cycles a,b and a balanced solution of (3) for each target u=ej−en−1, 0≤j<n−1, where ej is a coordinate unit vector. These targets form a basis of Vn,m, including in characteristic two when m divides n. Indeed, any balanced vector u is ∑j<n−1uj⁢(ej−en−1). The linear combination of the stored solutions with these coefficients therefore solves the equation for u. The number of basis witnesses checked is

12⋅7⏟corners+39⋅11⏟nonidentity edge types=513.

For example, the corner identity type still has seven independent twist targets. The edge identity type uses a separate argument.

Coverage follows from cycle type in the full symmetric group. The catalogue includes the partitions λ of n for which n−ℓ⁢(λ) is even, omitting 112 only on the edge side. Lean checks these lists against the cycle types of the actual rows. Conjugating by a relabelling d sends (p,v) to (d⁢p⁢d−1,v∘d−1), so both balance and (3) transport to any labelling of the same type. The relabelling of one piece orbit need not itself be a physical move: it is a change of coordinates, and the resulting paired factors satisfy (1).

For pure edge flips, the formal proof uses three fixed six-element sets

P={0,1,2,3,4,5},Q={0,1,2,6,7,8},R=P△Q.

At least one of their three subset sums vanishes in 𝔽2, since the third is the sum of the first two. For each set a fixed alternating cycle and explicit offsets solve the equation whenever its sum vanishes. This covers all 211 balanced flip vectors. Finally the two permutation signs, the componentwise equality and the order calculation give the result in the subgroup G.

Reproducibility.

The ancillary files include the Lean sources, the finite witnesses and the dependency manifest. The optional generator searches for witnesses; Lean checks each row, its cycle label and the exhaustiveness assertion. With the pinned Lean 4.35.0 toolchain and mathlib revision in the manifest, run the following commands from the ancillary directory:

bash cache.sh
lake build CubeComm
lake env lean -DwarningAsError=true AuditPaper.lean
lake env leanchecker CubeComm

The audit checks the main theorem and its single-commutator corollary. Their transitive axiom dependencies are propositional extensionality, classical choice and quotient soundness.

Use of AI tools.

OpenAI Codex assisted in the preparation of the Lean development, the literature comparison, and the drafting of the mathematical exposition.

References

  • [1] P. Bader, B. Böhmler, and P. Wegener, Commutators of signed n-cycles, preprint, 2026. arXiv:2609.24518v1 [math.GR].
  • [2] T. Sun, Commutators in the Rubik’s Cube group, Amer. Math. Monthly 131 (2024), no. 1, 3–19. doi:10.1080/00029890.2023.2263158.
  • [3] A. Vavpetič, Commutators of cycles in permutation groups, Ars Math. Contemp. 10 (2016), no. 1, 67–77. doi:10.26493/1855-3974.430.eaf.
